So what kind of work do you actually want to do? And do not say helping people, everybody says helping people.
Fine. Something where the decision happens fast. To be more specific, where you find out within an hour whether you were right.
Okay, that is much better. Can you elaborate? Because that describes about forty jobs.
Then let me narrow it down. Work where the person in front of you is the whole problem, and there is no report to write about it afterwards.
Now that is a real answer. Where does that come from? Somebody you know?
A coach I had in Franca, whose whole method was deciding in five seconds and living with it. He was wrong a lot, and it did not seem to cost him anything.
And that is the part you actually admired, isn’t it. Not the deciding. The living with it.
Yes. Which is to say I am not sure any of this is about work at all. What about you — what did you say when people asked you that at eighteen?
Franca, which is famous for basketball, is the city where I grew up.
The coach who trained me in Franca still messages me.
Could you elaborate on that? I am not sure which part you mean.

You asked me who mattered, and the honest answer is somebody whose name I had to look up last year, because I had forgotten it. She taught the class I was failing, which was not the class I cared about, and she kept me back one afternoon and asked me a question that nobody had asked. She did not ask what I wanted to be. She asked what kind of day I wanted to have, over and over, for forty years. That is a different question and it has a different answer. Everything I have chosen since came out of that afternoon, which is to say out of about eleven minutes with a teacher whose subject I never used again.

When somebody gives me a vague answer I no longer assume they are hiding something. Usually they are being careful. A vague sentence is the widest true thing a person can say, and widening is what you do when you are not sure the narrow version is true. So the useful move is not to accuse them of being vague. It is to offer them a narrower sentence and let them correct it. You said you want to help people. Do you mean one person at a time, or do you mean systems? Almost nobody answers that with a shrug. And the version they give you back is never the one you offered, which is the point: they had the precise answer the whole time, and what they were missing was permission to be wrong in public.

In 2017 a group of delivery drivers in the United States won a case about overtime pay, and the entire argument was about one missing comma. The rule listed the kinds of work that did not qualify for overtime, and one item read, roughly, packing for shipment or distribution. The company said that meant two separate activities, packing and distribution, and that driving counted as distribution. The drivers said it meant one activity: packing, for the purpose of shipment or distribution. Without a comma, both readings are available, and the court agreed that the drivers reading was at least as good. The state added the comma the following year. It is the clearest example anybody has of something English teachers say and nobody believes: punctuation is not decoration. It is where the meaning lives.
